A Note to the Reader

Seeing Ghana Clearly

Ghana stands at a remarkable inflection point. After decades of steady economic growth disrupted by fiscal imbalances and external shocks, the country is navigating a decisive period of reform, recovery, and repositioning.

The 2025 IMF Extended Credit Facility — the largest in Ghana's history — has imposed a fiscal discipline that, while painful in the short term, is creating the macroeconomic stability that private capital requires. Inflation, which peaked at 54% in late 2022, has declined substantially. The cedi has stabilized. And the 2026 national budget, with GH₵6.9 billion earmarked for oil palm development alone, signals a government turning decisively toward productive sector investment.

This report is designed for the Ghanaian business leader, the international investor, the development partner, and the global professional who wants to understand not just that Ghana has potential — but precisely where that potential is most actionable, most urgent, and most aligned with real human flourishing.

BRIDGE takes a systems view. We do not invest in sectors in isolation. We map the connections between infrastructure and agriculture, between financial inclusion and technology, between education and manufacturing. This integrated approach is what distinguishes a development intelligence organization from a traditional investment fund — and what makes the BRIDGE portfolio more than the sum of its parts.

The question is no longer whether Ghana's development opportunity is real. The question is who will organize the capital, expertise, and relationships to make it tangible.

Section One Macro Context

Ghana at a Crossroads

The structural forces shaping Ghana's development decade — and the macroeconomic case for acting now

In the early 2000s, Ghana was celebrated as Africa's democratic model — stable, growing, with transparent elections. By 2022, the country was navigating its worst fiscal crisis in a generation. What follows that kind of disruption, when handled well, is opportunity.

Ghana experienced the boom-bust pattern common to commodity-dependent economies: oil revenues from the Jubilee Field discovery fueled public spending that was never reined in when revenues disappointed. But Ghana's underlying productive sectors — agriculture, manufacturing, technology, and services — never fully caught up with consumption growth. The country remained a raw-material exporter, processing very little domestically, importing what it could produce, leaving structural value gaps across every sector.

What is emerging from the IMF adjustment process is a macroeconomic foundation that sophisticated investors recognize as a precondition for productive capital deployment. This is the alignment moment BRIDGE was built for.

2026 Budget Signal

Ghana's 2026 national budget allocates GH₵8.9B to productive sector investment across agriculture, infrastructure, education, health, and technology — creating direct co-investment opportunities for BRIDGE across all 12 sectors.

Section Two BRIDGE Thesis

The BRIDGE Thesis

12 integrated sectors, one unified mission — Peace & Prosperity for every Ghanaian

Most development initiatives fail not because the analysis is wrong, but because the intervention is too narrow. BRIDGE was designed around a single insight: Ghana's development challenges are interconnected, and so must be their solutions.

A microfinance program puts capital in farmers' hands — but without cold storage, the harvest still rots. A technology platform digitizes market transactions — but without road access, traders cannot reach the market. A health facility is built — but without reliable power, it cannot operate after dark.

BRIDGE's twelve-sector framework is not a list of investment themes — it is a map of an integrated system, where each sector both contributes to and depends on the others. Our portfolio is structured around four strategic pillars: Foundation Sectors that provide the physical and financial substrate; Human Capital Sectors that develop people; Economic Engine Sectors that create productive activity and employment; and Growth Engine Sectors that amplify returns and create new categories of opportunity.

Peace and Prosperity: enabling individuals to live with dignity, families to build security, and communities to thrive together.

Infrastructure & Basic Services

From Kejetia Market to rural connectivity — the physical substrate of Ghanaian prosperity

The Kejetia Opportunity

West Africa's largest market — Kejetia in Kumasi — houses over 10,000 traders processing hundreds of millions of cedis in daily transactions, almost entirely in cash, on paper, with no digital trail, no formal credit access, and no price discovery mechanism. This is BRIDGE's flagship infrastructure venture: a market digitization platform that transforms how commerce works at scale.

The model is replicable. Ghana has hundreds of major markets, all operating the same way. Each represents a venue for financial inclusion, logistics optimization, and SME formalization — if the infrastructure for digital commerce exists.

Market Digitization

Kejetia and 400+ major markets operating on paper. Digital platforms enable financial inclusion, price transparency, and SME credit access at scale.

WASH Infrastructure

7,653 preventable deaths annually. Communities, schools, and clinics lack safe water and sanitation systems — solvable with targeted capital deployment.

Digital Connectivity

EUR 155M government investment in rural connectivity (2,016 new sites) creates last-mile platform deployment opportunities across the BRIDGE portfolio.

Sector Spotlight · 06 Agriculture

Agriculture & Value Chains

Transforming $1.9 billion in annual post-harvest losses into rural household prosperity

Every year, Ghanaian farmers grow enough food to feed the nation many times over. And every year, approximately $1.9 billion worth of that food rots before it can be sold — on farm tracks, in unrefrigerated trucks, in markets without cold storage.

Post-harvest loss rates by crop: current vs. BRIDGE intervention target. Field trials show maize loss reduced from 36.7% to 3.1% with appropriate storage technology. Source: BRIDGE Sector Analysis, 2026.

Where the Value Goes

Ghana's smallholder farmers receive only 20–40% of the final consumer price for their produce. The remaining 60–80% is captured by an intermediary chain operating without refrigeration, quality standards, or formal contracts. BRIDGE's agricultural thesis targets the aggregation, storage, and processing layers — not to displace existing actors, but to formalize and upgrade them, enabling higher throughput and better value distribution back to farmers.

2026 Budget Signal

GH₵6.9B allocated for Oil Palm Development — the largest single agricultural investment in Ghana's recent history. BRIDGE is positioned as co-financing partner and service delivery operator with a 5-year moratorium on repayment.

The Processing Gap

Ghana is the world's second-largest cocoa producer — 800,000+ farm families, $2B+ in annual foreign exchange — yet processes only 20–30% domestically. The government has set a target of 50% domestic processing by 2030. This pattern repeats across shea, cashew, vegetables, and aquaculture. Each represents a distinct BRIDGE processing opportunity where capital, management, and market linkages can unlock value that already exists in the ground.

Sector Spotlight · 04 Technology

Technology & Innovation

Mobile-first, data-driven, and poised for Ghana's digital development leap

When M-PESA launched in Kenya in 2007, it transformed not just payments but the architecture of the entire economy. Ghana's mobile money market — 23.4 million users, the most active in Africa per capita — is that same kind of platform infrastructure waiting for its application layer.

Mobile-first is not a design choice — it is the structural reality of Ghana's digital economy.

The Platform Opportunity

Ghana's government has committed EUR 155M to rural connectivity, targeting 2,016 new telecom sites and 80% 4G penetration by 2028. The Next-Gen Infrastructure Company (NGIC) plans 4,400 new sites. Google's Equiano and 2Africa cables provide significantly upgraded international bandwidth. As this infrastructure deploys, the addressable market for digital services in Ghana will more than double.

BRIDGE's technology thesis focuses on the application layer — platforms that use this connectivity infrastructure to solve specific sector problems: AgriTech linking farmers to buyers, HealthTech enabling telemedicine to close the 1:6,000 physician gap, FinTech extending credit to the 40% unserved.

Ghana has 23.4 million mobile money users — Africa's leading market per capita. The infrastructure is built. BRIDGE is focused on the application layer that converts connectivity into prosperity.

Section Seven Budget Alignment

2026 Budget Alignment

When government capital and private capital flow into the same sectors, risk-adjusted returns improve and deployment timelines compress

The 2026 Ghanaian national budget is not simply a fiscal document — it is a signal. For the first time in several budget cycles, the allocation mix has shifted meaningfully toward productive sector investment.

Agriculture, energy, manufacturing, infrastructure, and technology all receive increased allocations. This creates a rare alignment between government co-investment capacity and BRIDGE's sector priorities. BRIDGE investments structured alongside public capital benefit from improved risk profiles, faster deployment timelines, and policy protection.

Co-investing alongside government capital is not just risk management — it is alignment strategy. When private capital flows into the same sectors as public capital, the probability of systemic improvement compounds.
